title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Monday evening, Nov 23
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 5:30 PM ET Monday, Nov 23, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). The Right had the day. The 'Tarlov admits the fine people hoax' story kept climbing (14,758 posts in 24 hours, up from 8,467 this morning; 6,331 from 7 AM to 5 PM ET) as Mediaite picked it up. Two new Right cards: a Michigan claim that a Chinese-made Wi-Fi radio was broadcasting next to a Dominion tabulator went from 3 posts in Sunday's daytime hours to 5,000 in Monday's, almost all after 1 PM, as Republicans asked CISA to investigate; and Trump's Sunday post that 'Somalians have completely taken over' Minnesota and 'almost 95% are on some form of welfare' kept a 19,652-post query running. The forensic-audit demand rose again in daytime hours (5,244 versus 4,214 Sunday), and the Rikers attack picked up a new '$500 a month to house criminals' frame. On the Far Left, Medicare for All is still the biggest query (26,979 posts) but cooled from Sunday's Meet the Press peak, and Van Hollen vs. Schumer fell to about its weekly average.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 5:07 PM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). Tech and entertainment dominated: 'Jensen' (712,113 posts), 'Nvidia' (581,471), 'Doomsday' (452,058), 'X-Men' (153,548), 'National Security' (58,672) and 'Chinese Spy' (38,593), mostly about Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang and Schumer's announced probe. Political names on the list included 'Eric Swalwell' (8,869), 'Bill Clinton' (3,202), 'Jimmy Gomez' (3,428), 'Rob Sand' (2,273), 'Scott Galloway' (2,135), 'House Ethics Committee' (1,406) and 'Feinstein' (no count). None matched a card in this set, so no card gets the trend bonus this evening. 'Jessica Tarlov,' on the list this morning, was not. Where a trend object had no tweet_count, its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The Rikers card is a Right attack on a Democratic mayor; we include it because Mamdani is being used as the national face of the party. The market card is tagged Right because the 'Democrats crashed the market' frame comes from Trump and his Treasury Secretary, even though many posts matching the query are rebuttals. The Rubio card recasts the incoming majority as Marxist, using a 2020 video. The 'fine people' card is tagged Right because it uses a Fox co-host's comment to brand Democrats as liars; it is about a 2017 quote, not the midterms. The Rahm Emanuel card is tagged Far Left because the narrative is the left's backlash to a centrist Democrat, even though Emanuel's remarks also circulate on the Right as proof of a Democratic civil war. The Medicare for All card is tagged Far Left because the pressure is on Jeffries, Schumer and the incoming majority to deliver it now. The Van Hollen card is tagged Far Left because the push to replace Schumer comes from the party's left. The tag is the primary opposition frame. The new Michigan Wi-Fi card is tagged Right because the claim casts doubt on an election Democrats won. The new Somali–Minnesota card is tagged Right because it is Trump's attack on a community in a Democratic-run state.

methodology: Last updated Monday, Nov 23, 2026, 5:30 PM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 5:07 PM ET. This morning's snapshot (Nov 23, 7:20 AM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Eight of its ten narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps this morning's by 14 hours (5 PM Sunday to 7 AM Monday ET), so we also report each query's 7 AM–5 PM ET daytime count against the same hours Sunday. Two narratives were dropped because they faded: the Obama 'country club' card (970 posts in the last 24 hours, down from 1,616 this morning; 307 from 7 AM to 5 PM ET versus 953 the same hours Sunday) and the Stephen A. Smith 'Democrats import voters' card (2,286, 0.79× its prior daily average; 1,047 versus 2,221). Two were added with new queries: the Michigan Wi-Fi tabulator claim and Trump's Somali–Minnesota post. The Somali query had large volume before Trump's post (8,699 posts in Sunday's 7 AM–5 PM hours), so its acceleration is modest. Other stories in X News this afternoon were not scored: Republican anger at Senate leader John Thune is an intra-Republican fight, and Democrats' plans on Iran war funding, tax cuts and the DNC's 2028 debate rules were covered as news rather than as opposition narratives.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 166-hour window from 7:00 PM ET Monday, Nov 16, through 5:00 PM ET Monday, Nov 23 (the 'seven-day' total), and used the last 24 hourly buckets (5:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 22, through 5:00 PM ET Monday, Nov 23) for the 24-hour count and hourly chart. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, transcripts, advocacy groups, blogs, aggregators, archives, X News summaries and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; this evening that includes the Election Crime Bureau, Badlands Media, SmokeScreen and a Truth Social archive. This evening we researched the two new cards and re-researched the 'fine people,' audit, Rikers, Medicare for All and Rahm Emanuel cards; the other cards carry this morning's outlet counts and say so. No card in this set matched the U.S. trends list this evening.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list when we pulled it. No card got the trend bonus this evening (the 'fine people' card had it this morning). The 'fine people,' Michigan Wi-Fi, Rubio and Rahm Emanuel queries had tiny baselines earlier in the week, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out. The Medicare for All and Van Hollen queries already carried large daily volumes all week, which keeps their acceleration modest. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Morning-to-evening score changes also reflect the volume ceiling (26,979 this evening versus 32,796 this morning), the loss of the trend bonus, and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The Michigan Wi-Fi query requires a Wi-Fi term plus Dominion, tabulator, 'voting machine' or 'Martin Township,' so it also catches rebuttals. The Somali query requires Somali, Somalis or Somalia plus Minnesota, Minneapolis or 'taken over,' so it catches news relays, rebuttals and posts about the Minnesota fraud cases and other Somali news. The audit query catches posts mocking the demand and posts about the separate RNC spending-audit fight. The market query requires a market term plus 'Democrats' or 'blue wave,' so it also catches rebuttals and general market posts that mention Democrats. The 'fine people' query requires 'fine people' or Charlottesville plus hoax, Tarlov, 'The Five,' Biden or context, so it also catches posts defending the original reading. The Rahm Emanuel query includes the bare name 'Rahm' and terms like 2028. The Rikers query also catches straight news posts and rebuttals. The Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and general health-care posts, and its 'M4A' term can catch unrelated uses. The Van Hollen query catches syndicated news posts. The Rubio query catches any post pairing 'democratic socialism' with Marxism or communism, including posts from other countries. Replies are included. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples (7 AM to 5 PM ET Monday) and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This evening we pulled fresh samples for the Michigan Wi-Fi, Somali, 'fine people,' audit and Rikers queries. The other cards carry this morning's sentiment and say so. disinfo.caveatBody: New this evening: the Michigan 'Chinese Wi-Fi radio next to a Dominion tabulator' claim does not show a tabulator was connected to anything. The Election Crime Bureau's own write-up says the tabulator model in use has no internal modem and the system is certified with no wireless technology, and the hotspot's name matches a consumer wireless-display adapter; Lead Stories rated Patrick Colbeck's earlier Election Day version Unsupported, and Michigan's Department of State called it 'complete nonsense.' The sheriff's review it cites has not reported findings. Trump's 'Somalians have completely taken over… Minnesota… almost 95% are on some form of welfare' is false on scale and unsupported on the number: Somali Minnesotans are roughly 1–2 percent of the state, and the state demographer's figure for any public assistance, mostly Medicaid, was 84% (FactCheck.org); PolitiFact found his earlier '92% don't work' wrong. 'Mamdani will pay families to house the criminals he releases' describes a real program in a misleading way: the Kinship Reentry Housing Program started in 2021, pays $500 a month for up to 12 months to families housing a relative coming home, and the plan would grow it from 50 to 300 families (New York Post; NYC Mayor's Office). Carried over from this morning: 'Jessica Tarlov admitted the "very fine people" hoax' gets the narrow point right and the conclusion wrong. Trump did say he was 'not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists,' and Snopes rated the claim that he called them 'very fine people' False; but Snopes also notes the Unite the Right rally was conceived, led and attended by white supremacists, so 'very fine people on both sides' was itself inaccurate, and one commentator's podcast remark is not evidence that Democrats invented the quote. Bessent's 'the sell-off began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls' is his reading of the timing, not a measured cause; in the same answer he cited hawkish Fed remarks and tighter financial conditions (CBS News transcript), and coverage ties the drop to the AI sell-off, the Anthropic IPO and Nvidia's turmoil as well as to expected data-center rules (NPR; The Hill). Page Twenty One finds Trump's 'more than $6 trillion' roughly right on a total-market basis, 'Nasdaq down 20%' exaggerated (about 10.9% from the Nov. 3 close to Nov. 20) and '100% due to the Democrats' not supported. Trump's 'NASDAQ, by itself, is down 20%' since the Nov. 3 midterms is wrong. From the last close before the vote (Nov. 2) to Friday's close the Nasdaq Composite fell 10.1%, the S&P 500 8.4% and the Dow 7.4% (Mediaite; MODEL, checking Nasdaq index data); the Composite is 18.1% below its Oct. 6 record, and the Nasdaq-100 is 19.8% below its record. '100% due to the Democrats' leaves out the AI and chip sell-off and the turmoil at Nvidia that coverage ties last week's drop to (The Hill), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. The viral Marco Rubio 'Democratic socialism… is Marxism' video is from Feb. 24, 2020, when he was a senator commenting on Bernie Sanders's primary campaign (Political Wire; The Right Scoop), not a response to this month's election. 'El-Sayed abandoned Medicare for All' is overstated: he said on Meet the Press he supports Sanders's bill but prefers a version that keeps private plans available (NBC News; POLITICO). 'Forensic-audit all 50 states before certifying' is misleading. Every state already has a post-election audit procedure (NCSL, via Votebeat), Texas began its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the U.S. Senate race on Nov. 19 (Houston Public Media), and audits and certification are separate processes that can run in parallel (The Crosscheck, which rated the 'don't certify until verified' claim Misleading). Earlier viral fraud claims, a Houston 'FBI raid' and a Wyandot County, Ohio, tally error, were debunked by PolitiFact and AFP. 'Medicare for All saves 114,000 lives and $1 trillion a year' is a projection from a Yale preprint that has not been peer reviewed; about 51,300 of those lives come from reversing coverage cuts enacted since 2025, not from single-payer itself, and the model leaves out transition costs (Yale School of Public Health; Renaissance Physician). Trump's 'Democrats Hurt Stocks' chart gets the numbers right and the cause wrong. The S&P 500 did fall 8.7% from the Nov. 3 close to the Nov. 20 close, and total U.S.-listed market value fell about $7.7 trillion (Candid Dragon's chatter check), but stocks rallied the day after the results, Friday's drop is tied mainly to the Nvidia accounting-probe report and the AI sell-off (Reuters; CNBC), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. 'Democrats are importing immigrants to replace Black voters' is Stephen A. Smith's stated belief, not an established fact: the census does count every resident for House seats, as the Constitution requires, but noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and PolitiFact has rated the related claim that millions of immigrants are registering to vote Pants on Fire. 'Trump endorsed Medicare for All' is overstated: he reposted El-Sayed's 'TrumpCare' card and praised Democrats' health-care ideas but has not backed a bill. 'Mamdani is releasing thousands of criminals' and 'Mamdani is closing Rikers now' get the plan backward: it sets a target of no more than 4,100 people in custody by the end of 2032, reached through diversion and shorter case delays, keeps Rikers open until borough jails are built, and asks the City Council to move the legal deadline later, from August 2027 to 2032 (City of New York; City & State; Gothamist). 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading.

Michigan won't audit the machines, so CISA has to.

narratives.audience: 2020 election skeptics and Lindell followers; Michigan Republicans angry about the midterm losses; China hawks; and casual readers who see 'Dominion' and 'Chinese Wi-Fi' in the same sentence.

If the sheriff is looking at it, let that finish and publish what it finds. Then point to Michigan's post-election audits and paper ballots, which can be hand-checked whatever a Wi-Fi scanner shows.

On ABC's This Week on Sunday, former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a possible 2028 candidate, said of the 11 House Democrats who voted against Hakeem Jeffries's speaker nomination: 'Give me a break… You're like the Green Party and the Libertarian Party. I'll see you in November,' and 'they literally don't understand the Democratic Party. They're not part of the Democratic Party because we are a coalition' (ABC News transcript). At least seven of the 11 are from the party's left wing (The Washington Post), and DSA's national organization said it 'stands with the members-elect who voted NO' and wants 'no more corporate coronations' (DSA statement). talkingPoints: Rahm says we're 'not part of the Democratic Party.' Then stop asking for our votes.
Voting no on Jeffries wasn't about race; it was about 'no more corporate coronations.'
Rahm and Carville are auditioning the 2016 playbook for 2028.
The people who lost to Trump don't get to lecture the people who just won.
narratives.amplifiers: Left: DSA's national statement backing the members-elect who voted no, progressive reply accounts, and critics of Carville's praise for Emanuel. Also spread by ABC News's own clips and by Right outlets (Gateway Pundit) using it to show a Democratic civil war.
narratives.whyItWorks: It gives the left a villain who stands for the party's donor wing at the moment DSA is claiming credit for the wave. Emanuel's lines — comparing DSA to the Green and Libertarian parties and invoking 'defunding the police, open borders, open prisons' — confirm the left's belief that centrists see them as a liability, and his 2028 ambitions make every remark read as a campaign move.
narratives.audience: DSA members and younger progressive voters; supporters of the 11 members-elect who voted against Jeffries; and Black Democrats who agree with Emanuel that the Jeffries vote mattered, which is why the fight cuts both ways.
narratives.counter: Avoid amplifying a personality fight. Note what both sides agree on — Emanuel and DSA both want Schumer to step aside, and both talk about corruption and the minimum wage — and point the energy at the agenda that won in November. Jeffries is expected to win the speaker vote in January either way.

New this evening: daytime posts rose (4,040 from 7 AM to 5 PM ET versus 3,074 the same hours Sunday) on a new frame from a Nov. 21 New York Post story: the 88-page Close Rikers plan would expand the Kinship Reentry Housing Program, started in 2021, from 50 to 300 families, with $3.55 million this fiscal year and $7.1 million in later years. The Osborne Association, which runs it, now pays families $500 a month for up to 12 months to house a relative coming home from jail or prison, with counseling and case management. Posts recast that as Mamdani 'paying people to house criminals he releases'; the plan targets a jail population of no more than 4,100 by its 2032 closing date, down from about 6,600 (NYC Mayor's Office). talkingPoints: Mamdani wants to pay families $500 a month to house the inmates he lets out.
Mamdani is closing Rikers and letting thousands of criminals out.
You can't cut the jail population by 2,500 without releasing people charged with violent crimes.
First he cut the NYPD's protest unit, now he empties the jails.
This is what a Democratic socialist city looks like — and Democrats want it everywhere.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), @EricLDaugh (101,116 views), @WescottAmerica, @Helen4NY, New York Post opinion pages, and the Correction Officers' Benevolent Association. News coverage: AP, POLITICO, Gothamist, City & State and BBC. Supporters include Council Members Sandy Nurse and Tiffany Cabán and Council Speaker Julie Menin, who backs a 'responsible transition.'
narratives.whyItWorks: Crime and disorder are the Right's most reliable attack on big-city Democrats, and Mamdani is the most visible democratic socialist in office, so a jail story in New York becomes a national preview of 'Democratic rule.' Specific-sounding numbers (2,100, 2,500, 7,000) turn a six-year population target into an image of open cell doors. It also pairs with other Mamdani stories circulating Friday, such as his NYPD unit cut and his pitch for monthly DSA donations, to build a single picture.
narratives.audience: Outer-borough and suburban New Yorkers worried about crime, national conservative audiences who see Mamdani as the face of the Democratic left, and police and corrections-officer communities.
narratives.counter: Nobody is opening the doors on Friday. The plan sets a population target for the end of 2032, reached through diversion, supervised release and faster cases, and Rikers stays open until the borough jails are built (City of New York; Gothamist). Closing Rikers has been city law since 2019, passed under de Blasio; this plan actually pushes the deadline later, and it still needs City Council approval (AP). Take the real question seriously: critics doubt the target can be met safely, so answer with how many people are held on lower-level charges and how case delays will be cut, not with slogans.
